questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following is a unit of length?

solution.concept: Units of length used for very large distances
solution.explanation: A light year is the distance light travels in vacuum in one year (about 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m), so it measures length, not time. The kilowatt hour and the electron volt are units of energy, and the poise is the CGS unit of the coefficient of viscosity.
steps: Light year = speed of light × one year → a distance
kWh and eV → energy; poise → viscosity
solution.why_others_wrong: Kilowatt hour (3.6 × 10⁶ J) and electron volt (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) are energy units; the poise is a unit of viscosity. The word 'year' misleads students into treating the light year as a unit of time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', the international system of units

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (combination of physical quantities) with List-II (its dimensional formula).

List-I:
A. Pressure divided by density
B. Force divided by the product of a length and a speed
C. Square root of (Young's modulus divided by density)
D. Angular momentum divided by linear momentum

List-II:
I. [L]
II. [L² T⁻²]
III. [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹]
IV. [L T⁻¹]

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Dimensions of derived combinations
solution.explanation: Pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²] ÷ density [M L⁻³] = [L² T⁻²]. Force [M L T⁻²] ÷ (length × speed) [L² T⁻¹] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹], the dimensions of the coefficient of viscosity. Young's modulus has the dimensions of pressure, so √(Y/ρ) = √[L² T⁻²] = [L T⁻¹], a speed. Angular momentum [M L² T⁻¹] ÷ linear momentum [M L T⁻¹] = [L].
steps: A: [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]/[M L⁻³] = [L² T⁻²] → II
B: [M L T⁻²]/[L² T⁻¹] = [M L⁻¹ T⁻¹] → III
D: [M L² T⁻¹]/[M L T⁻¹] = [L] → I
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes either forget to take the square root in C (giving [L² T⁻²] instead of a speed) or swap the viscosity-type combination B with a length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', dimensions of physical quantities
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The volume of a small sphere is to be found from its measured radius, using V = (4/3)πr³. If the maximum percentage error in the volume must not exceed 1.2%, the largest permissible percentage error in measuring the radius is:

solution.concept: Propagation of relative error through a power
solution.explanation: For a quantity Z = k rⁿ, the maximum relative error is ΔZ/Z = n Δr/r; the constant 4π/3 has no error. Here n = 3, so the percentage error in V is three times that in r. Working backwards, the error allowed in r is one-third of the error allowed in V.
solution.shortcut: Allowed error in the measured quantity = allowed error in the result ÷ power.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.6% multiplies by the power instead of dividing; 1.2% ignores the power; 0.6% divides by 2 as if the volume depended on r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', combination of errors (quantity raised to a power)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The speed v of short ripples on the surface of a liquid is assumed to depend only on the surface tension S of the liquid, its density ρ and the wavelength λ of the ripples, as v ∝ Sˣ ρʸ λᶻ. By the method of dimensions, the values of x, y and z are respectively:

solution.concept: Deducing a relation by dimensional analysis
solution.explanation: S has dimensions [M T⁻²] (force per unit length), ρ is [M L⁻³] and λ is [L]. Equate powers of M, L and T on both sides of [L T⁻¹] = [M T⁻²]ˣ [M L⁻³]ʸ [L]ᶻ.
solution.why_others_wrong: (1/2, −1/2, 1/2) makes a sign slip in the L equation; (1, −1, −1) gives [L² T⁻²], the square of a speed; (−1/2, 1/2, −1/2) inverts the T equation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', deducing relations among physical quantities

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A student finds g from g = 4π²L/T² for a simple pendulum whose period T is about 2 s. She measures T by timing n complete oscillations with a stopwatch of resolution 0.2 s and dividing the time by n. The length L is known very accurately. The least number of oscillations she must time so that the timing error contributes at most 1% to the maximum percentage error in g is:

solution.concept: Reducing the error of a measured period by timing many oscillations
solution.explanation: The total time t = nT ≈ 2n s is measured with an absolute error of 0.2 s, so Δt/t = 0.2/(2n). The period T = t/n has the same relative error. Since g ∝ T⁻², the relative error in g is twice that in T.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 forgets the factor 2 from T²; 40 is more than needed (it would keep the error within 0.5%); 5 oscillations would leave a timing error of 4% in g.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Units and Measurement', errors in measurement and combination of errors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body moves along a straight line with uniform acceleration. Its velocity is 10 m/s at t = 2 s and 20 m/s at t = 6 s, in the same direction. Its displacement between t = 2 s and t = 6 s is:

solution.concept: Average velocity under uniform acceleration
solution.explanation: For uniform acceleration the average velocity over an interval is the mean of the initial and final velocities, (10 + 20)/2 = 15 m/s. Displacement = average velocity × time = 15 × 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 m uses the final velocity for the whole interval; 40 m uses the initial velocity; 120 m adds the two velocities without halving.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The unit vector in the direction of the vector A = 6î − 8k̂ is:

solution.concept: Unit vector along a given vector
solution.explanation: A unit vector along A is Â = A/|A|. Here |A| = √(6² + 8²) = 10, so Â = (6î − 8k̂)/10.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.6î + 0.8k̂ loses the minus sign of the k̂ component; dividing by 14 adds the components instead of taking the magnitude; 0.8î − 0.6k̂ swaps the components.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', unit vectors and resolution of vectors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The position–time graph of a particle moving along the x-axis is a straight line parallel to the time axis, at x = +5 m. Over this interval the particle is:

options.text: Moving with a constant velocity of 5 m/s
Moving with a constant speed but changing direction

solution.concept: Reading a position–time graph
solution.explanation: The slope of a position–time graph is the velocity. A line parallel to the time axis has zero slope: the position does not change with time, so the particle is at rest at x = 5 m.
steps: Horizontal line → slope 0 → v = 0 at x = 5 m
solution.why_others_wrong: A constant velocity of 5 m/s would need a straight line with slope 5 m/s, not a horizontal line; constant acceleration gives a parabola; a particle moving along a line must change its x if it moves at all.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', position–time graphs
solution.final_answer: Option A: At rest at x = 5 m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground with an initial velocity whose horizontal component is 10 m/s and whose vertical component is 20 m/s upward. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, after how much time is its velocity directed at 45° below the horizontal?

solution.concept: Direction of velocity of a projectile
solution.explanation: The horizontal component stays 10 m/s. The velocity is at 45° below the horizontal when the vertical component is 10 m/s downward, i.e. v_y = 20 − 10t = −10 m/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 s gives 45° above the horizontal (on the way up); 2 s is the highest point, where the velocity is horizontal; 4 s is the time of flight, when the velocity is at 63° below the horizontal.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A swimmer who can swim at 5 m/s relative to still water swims 400 m straight upstream along a river and then swims back to her starting point. The river flows at a uniform 3 m/s. The total time for the round trip is:

solution.concept: Relative velocity along a line: motion in a flowing river
solution.explanation: Relative to the ground, her speed is 5 − 3 = 2 m/s upstream and 5 + 3 = 8 m/s downstream. The times for the two legs are added; the current does not cancel out.
solution.why_others_wrong: 160 s ignores the current; 200 s counts only the upstream leg; 100 s uses 8 m/s for both legs.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Straight Line', relative velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A particle moves with constant speed along a circle of radius 0.5 m. Its velocity vector turns through 60° every 0.5 s. The magnitude of its centripetal acceleration is:

solution.concept: Angular speed and centripetal acceleration
solution.explanation: In uniform circular motion the velocity turns through the same angle as the radius vector, so the angular speed is ω = (π/3)/0.5 = 2π/3 rad/s. The centripetal acceleration is ω²r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4π²/9 m/s² is ω² without the radius; 8π²/9 m/s² uses ω²/r; 2π/3 is the angular speed itself (in rad/s, not an acceleration).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', uniform circular motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The component of a vector along a direction can be greater in magnitude than the vector itself.
Statement II: If the angle between two non-zero vectors A and B is greater than 90°, then |A − B| is greater than |A + B|.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Components of a vector; magnitudes of sum and difference
solution.explanation: The component of A along a unit vector n̂ is A cos θ, and |cos θ| ≤ 1, so a component can never exceed the magnitude: Statement I is false. |A ± B|² = A² + B² ± 2AB cos θ; for θ > 90°, cos θ < 0, so the difference has the larger magnitude: Statement II is true.
steps: Component = A cos θ ≤ A → I false
|A − B|² − |A + B|² = −4AB cos θ > 0 for θ > 90° → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I contradicts |cos θ| ≤ 1, so the options calling it true are wrong; Statement II follows directly from the law of vector addition, so the options calling it false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', addition of vectors and resolution of vectors
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The scalar (dot) product of two non-zero vectors can be negative.
Reason (R): The scalar product of two vectors is commutative, that is, A · B = B · A.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Scalar product: sign and commutativity
solution.explanation: A · B = AB cos θ. For 90° < θ ≤ 180°, cos θ is negative, so the scalar product is negative: A is true. The scalar product is indeed commutative, so R is true; but commutativity says nothing about the sign of the product. The sign comes from cos θ, which R does not mention.
steps: A · B = AB cos θ < 0 when θ > 90° → A true
A · B = B · A → R true
R does not explain the sign → B
solution.why_others_wrong: R is a separate property of the dot product, not the reason it can be negative, so A is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane' (and 'Work, Energy and Power'), scalar product
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body moving along a straight line with uniform acceleration covers 24 m in a certain interval of 4 s and 64 m in the next 4 s. Its velocity at the start of the first interval and its acceleration are respectively:

solution.concept: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion over successive equal intervals
solution.explanation: Write s = ut + ½at² for the first 4 s and for the first 8 s (24 + 64 = 88 m). Alternatively, for successive equal intervals T the distances differ by aT².
steps: Subtract twice the first: 16a = 40 → a = 2.5 m/s²
solution.why_others_wrong: (4, 1) treats 64 m as the distance covered in the whole 8 s; (6, 2.5) takes the average speed 24/4 as the initial velocity; (−4, 5) uses s₂ − s₁ = ½aT².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball is projected from level ground. When it is 15 m above the ground on its way up, its velocity is (10î + 10ĵ) m/s, where î is horizontal and ĵ is vertically upward. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, its maximum height and its horizontal range are respectively:

solution.concept: Projectile motion: recovering the launch velocity from data at one point
solution.explanation: The horizontal component is 10 m/s throughout. For the vertical motion, v_y² = u_y² − 2gh gives the initial vertical component; then H = u_y²/2g and R = u_x × 2u_y/g.
steps: Time of flight = 2 × 20/10 = 4 s → R = 10 × 4 = 40 m
solution.why_others_wrong: (5 m, 20 m) treats the given velocity as the launch velocity; (20 m, 80 m) doubles the time of flight again; (15 m, 30 m) takes the given height as the maximum height.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The position vector of a particle moving in the x–y plane is r = (2t) î + (t² − 4t) ĵ, where r is in metres and t in seconds. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At t = 2 s, the velocity of the particle is along the +x direction.
(b) The acceleration of the particle is constant, of magnitude 2 m/s², along the +y direction.
(c) The speed of the particle is least at t = 0.
(d) The speed of the particle at t = 0 is 2√5 m/s.
(e) At t = 4 s, the particle is 4 m from the origin.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Velocity and acceleration from a position vector
solution.explanation: Differentiate: v = 2î + (2t − 4)ĵ and a = 2ĵ. Check each statement with these.
steps: (c) speed² = 4 + (2t − 4)² is least at t = 2 s, not t = 0 → false
(e) t = 4 s: r = 8î + 0ĵ, distance 8 m → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) confuse the start of the motion with the instant of least speed; options with (e) take the x-coordinate's coefficient instead of evaluating r at t = 4 s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Motion in a Plane', position, velocity and acceleration vectors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A car of mass 1500 kg moving at 20 m/s along a straight level road is brought to rest in 5 s by its brakes. The magnitude of the average force exerted on the car to stop it is:

solution.concept: Force as the rate of change of momentum
solution.explanation: The car's momentum changes from 1500 × 20 = 30 000 kg m/s to zero in 5 s. By Newton's second law the average force equals the change in momentum divided by the time taken.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 000 N is the momentum itself (units kg m/s, not a force); 300 N divides the mass by the time and leaves out the speed; 1500 N equates the force with the mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: According to Newton's first law, every body resists a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. The quantitative measure of this inertia of a body is its:

solution.concept: Inertia and mass
solution.explanation: Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its velocity. For the same force, a body of larger mass gets a smaller acceleration (a = F/m), so mass measures inertia. Velocity, acceleration and momentum describe the state of motion, not the resistance to changing it.
steps: Larger mass → harder to change velocity → mass measures inertia
solution.why_others_wrong: A body has the same inertia whether it is at rest (zero velocity and momentum) or moving, and whatever its acceleration, so these cannot measure inertia.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', Newton's first law of motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gun of mass 4 kg, free to move, fires a bullet of mass 20 g horizontally with a speed of 400 m/s. The recoil speed of the gun is:

solution.concept: Conservation of linear momentum in firing
solution.explanation: Before firing the total momentum of the gun–bullet system is zero. With no external horizontal force it stays zero, so the gun's momentum is equal and opposite to the bullet's: M V = m v.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 m/s divides 4 by 8 the wrong way round; 20 m/s and 8 m/s come from not converting 20 g to 0.020 kg consistently (20 m/s uses 0.2 kg, 8 m/s is the bullet's momentum taken as a speed).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A box of mass 11 kg rests on a rough horizontal floor; the coefficient of static friction is 0.5. A rope pulls it with a force directed at 37° above the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). Taking g = 10 m/s², the least pull that just starts the box sliding is:

solution.concept: Limiting friction with an inclined pull
solution.explanation: The upward component of the pull reduces the normal reaction: N = mg − F sin 37°. The box just starts to slide when the horizontal component equals the limiting friction μN.
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 N is the limiting friction for a horizontal pull; 110 N treats the pull as pressing the box down (N = mg + F sin θ); 68.75 N divides 55 N by cos 37° but keeps N = mg.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', friction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small bob tied to a light string 1 m long moves in a horizontal circle with constant speed, the string making a constant angle of 60° with the vertical (a conical pendulum). Taking g = 10 m/s², the speed of the bob is:

solution.concept: Newton's second law for a body in uniform circular motion
solution.explanation: The vertical component of the tension balances the weight, T cos θ = mg, and the horizontal component provides the centripetal force, T sin θ = mv²/r, where the radius of the circle is r = L sin θ.
solution.why_others_wrong: √(5√3) uses r = L cos θ; √10 sets v² = gL; √(10√3) takes the radius as the full string length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a body at rest explodes into exactly two fragments, the fragments move off in opposite directions along the same straight line.
Statement II: In an explosion, the total kinetic energy of the fragments just after the explosion equals the kinetic energy of the body just before it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Momentum and kinetic energy in an explosion
solution.explanation: The forces of the explosion are internal, so total momentum stays zero: p₁ + p₂ = 0, i.e. the two momenta are equal and opposite, along one line. Statement I is true. Kinetic energy is not conserved: it increases from zero, at the expense of chemical (internal) energy. Statement II is false.
steps: p₁ = −p₂ → opposite directions, same line → I true
solution.why_others_wrong: Momentum, not kinetic energy, is conserved in an explosion, so the options calling II true are wrong; Statement I follows from momentum conservation, so the options calling it false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', conservation of momentum
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
All quantities are in SI units. Match List-I with List-II (magnitude of the quantity).

List-I:
A. Linear momentum of a 2 kg body moving at 3 m/s
B. Impulse of a constant force of 4 N acting for 2 s
C. Average force needed to change the momentum of a body by 10 kg m/s in 5 s
D. Change in momentum of a 0.5 kg ball that hits a wall normally at 4 m/s and rebounds normally at 4 m/s

List-II:
I. 2
II. 4
III. 6
IV. 8

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Momentum, impulse and force
solution.explanation: p = mv; impulse = FΔt; average force = Δp/Δt; for a rebound the velocity reverses, so Δp = m(v − (−u)).
solution.why_others_wrong: Matching D to 2 (or C to 4) forgets that the ball's velocity reverses, so its momentum changes by 2mv, not mv; the other codes swap momentum with impulse.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 1 kg is placed in contact with the front vertical face of a cart (the face that looks in the direction of motion). The cart moves forward on a level road with a horizontal acceleration, so that the face pushes the block forward and nothing else holds the block. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the face is 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², the least acceleration of the cart for which the block does not slide down is:

solution.concept: Static friction and Newton's second law
solution.explanation: The face pushes the block forward with the normal force N, which alone gives the block its acceleration a: N = ma. Friction along the face, at most μN, must hold up the weight: μma ≥ mg.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 m/s² is μg, as if friction had to provide the acceleration; 10 m/s² ignores μ; 40 m/s² uses 2g/μ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform rope of mass 2 kg hangs vertically with a block of mass 3 kg tied to its lower end. The upper end of the rope is pulled upward so that the rope and block move up with an acceleration of 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension at the midpoint of the rope is:

solution.concept: Tension in a heavy rope: Newton's second law for a part of a system
solution.explanation: Consider everything below the midpoint: the block (3 kg) and the lower half of the rope (1 kg). The tension at the midpoint is the only upward force on this 4 kg part: T − 4g = 4a.
solution.why_others_wrong: 60 N is the pull at the top (whole 5 kg); 36 N is the tension at the bottom of the rope; 40 N ignores the acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A string fixed at both ends at the same level, with a weight hung from its midpoint, can never be made exactly horizontal, however large the tension in it.
Reason (R): At the midpoint, the vertical components of the tensions in the two halves must together balance the weight, and these components are zero if the string is horizontal.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Equilibrium of three concurrent forces
solution.explanation: If each half makes an angle θ with the horizontal, equilibrium of the midpoint gives 2T sin θ = W, so T = W/(2 sin θ). For θ → 0, T → ∞; no finite tension makes θ exactly zero. R states exactly this vertical balance, so it explains A.
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the condition that makes A true, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Laws of Motion', equilibrium of a particle
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A body of mass 2 kg, initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface, is acted on by a horizontal force F = 6t, where F is in newtons and t in seconds. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its linear momentum at t = 2 s is 12 kg m/s.
(b) Its velocity at t = 2 s is 6 m/s.
(c) The impulse of the force during the first 2 s is 12 N s.
(d) Its acceleration is constant.
(e) Its kinetic energy at t = 2 s is 72 J.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Impulse of a variable force
solution.explanation: Impulse = ∫F dt = ∫₀² 6t dt = 3t² |₀² = 12 N s, which equals the change in momentum from zero.
steps: (d) a = F/m = 3t, which grows with time → false
(e) KE = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J, not 72 J → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) use mv² instead of ½mv²; options with (d) treat the force as constant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Work by constant and variable force
questions.question_text: A block of mass 2 kg slides 5 m down a plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s², the work done on the block by gravity is:

solution.concept: Work done by a constant force
solution.explanation: W = F d cos φ, where φ is the angle between the weight (vertically down) and the displacement (along the incline). That angle is 60°, so W = mg × 5 × cos 60° = mg × (vertical drop).
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 J multiplies mg by the full length of the incline; 50√3 J uses cos 30° (the angle of the incline) instead of the angle between force and displacement; 25 J halves the result again.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', work

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A motorboat moves through still water at a constant speed of 10 m/s. The water exerts a resistive force of 1500 N on it. The power delivered by the engine to move the boat is:

solution.concept: Power as force × velocity
solution.explanation: At constant speed the forward force from the engine equals the resistive force, 1500 N. The power is the rate of doing work, P = F v.
solution.why_others_wrong: 150 W divides the force by the speed; 1.5 kW and 150 kW are slips by a factor of 10 in the product.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (moving body) with List-II (its kinetic energy).

List-I:
A. A body of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s
B. A body of mass 0.5 kg moving at 4 m/s
C. A body of mass 4 kg having linear momentum 8 kg m/s
D. A body of mass 3 kg having linear momentum 6 kg m/s

List-II:
I. 4 J
II. 6 J
III. 8 J
IV. 9 J

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kinetic energy in terms of speed and momentum
solution.explanation: K = ½mv² = p²/(2m).
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes use p²/m (doubling C and D) or swap the momentum-based cases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', kinetic energy
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ball of mass 1 kg moving at 6 m/s overtakes and collides head-on, elastically, with a ball of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s in the same direction along the same line. Their velocities just after the collision are respectively:

solution.concept: One-dimensional elastic collision with both bodies moving
solution.explanation: Conserve momentum, and use the fact that in a 1-D elastic collision the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach.
solution.why_others_wrong: (3, 6) simply exchanges the velocities, valid only for equal masses; (4, 4) is the perfectly inelastic result; (0, 6) conserves momentum but not kinetic energy (36 J ≠ 27 J).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', collisions in one dimension
solution.final_answer: Option B: 2 m/s and 5 m/s, both forward

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A stone of mass 0.2 kg is whirled in a vertical circle at the end of a light string 0.5 m long. The string breaks if its tension exceeds 22 N. Taking g = 10 m/s², the greatest speed the stone can have at the lowest point of the circle without the string breaking is:

solution.concept: Tension at the lowest point of a vertical circle
solution.explanation: At the lowest point the tension acts upward and the weight downward; their difference supplies the centripetal force: T − mg = mv²/L. The tension is greatest at the lowest point, so this is where the string would break first.
solution.why_others_wrong: √55 m/s ignores the weight; √60 m/s adds the weight instead of subtracting it; 10 m/s doubles the string length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a box is lifted vertically through a height h at a constant speed, the net work done on the box is zero, although the lifting force does work mgh on it.
Reason (R): By the work–energy theorem, the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy, which is zero when the speed does not change; the work +mgh of the lifting force is cancelled by the work −mgh done by gravity.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Work–energy theorem: net work and the work of individual forces
solution.explanation: At constant speed the lifting force equals mg, so it does work +mgh; gravity, acting opposite to the displacement, does −mgh. The total is zero, which agrees with the work–energy theorem since ΔK = 0. R gives exactly this reasoning, so it explains A.
steps: W_net = 0 = ΔK → R explains A → A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the very reason the net work is zero while one force does positive work, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the work–energy theorem
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two ideal springs A and B have spring constants k and 2k respectively. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) When both are stretched by the same force, the energy stored in A is twice that stored in B.
(b) When both are stretched by the same extension, the energy stored in B is twice that stored in A.
(c) When both are stretched by the same force, the extension of A is twice that of B.
(d) When both are stretched by the same extension, more work is done on A than on B.
(e) When both are stretched by the same force, they store equal energies.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Elastic potential energy of a spring: ½kx² = F²/2k
solution.explanation: For the same extension use U = ½kx², which is proportional to k. For the same force the extension is F/k, so U = F²/(2k), which is inversely proportional to k.
steps: (a) U ∝ 1/k at fixed F → U_A = 2U_B, true
(b) U ∝ k at fixed x → U_B = 2U_A, true
(d) work done = stored energy, larger for B → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) use the wrong one of the two forms ½kx² and F²/2k for the condition stated.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', the potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 1 kg is dropped from rest from a height of 0.4 m above the top of a light vertical spring of spring constant 1000 N/m, whose lower end is fixed to the floor. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, the maximum compression of the spring is:

solution.concept: Conservation of mechanical energy with a spring
solution.explanation: At maximum compression x the block is momentarily at rest. It has fallen a total height (0.4 + x), so the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the elastic energy stored: mg(h + x) = ½kx².
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.9 cm ignores the extra drop x during compression (mgh = ½kx²); 1 cm is the static compression mg/k; 20 cm doubles the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Work, Energy and Power', conservation of mechanical energy; potential energy of a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A bullet of mass 20 g moving horizontally at 500 m/s passes through a wooden block of mass 2 kg hanging at rest from a long light string, and emerges at 100 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting the loss of mass of the block, the maximum height through which the block rises is:

solution.concept: Momentum conservation in an inelastic collision followed by energy conservation
solution.explanation: During the very short passage the string force is vertical, so horizontal momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not (heat is produced in the wood). After that, the block swings up with its mechanical energy conserved.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.6 m uses h = V²/g; 0.05 m uses the bullet's exit momentum alone; 1.25 m treats the bullet as embedded in the block (V ≈ 4.95 m/s).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small bob of mass 0.2 kg hangs from a light inextensible string. The bob is pulled aside until the string is horizontal and taut, and is released from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², the tension in the string at the instant the string makes an angle of 60° with the vertical is:

solution.concept: Energy conservation and radial equation in a vertical circle
solution.explanation: When the string makes angle θ with the vertical, the bob has fallen L cos θ from the release level, so v² = 2gL cos θ. Along the string, T − mg cos θ = mv²/L.
solution.shortcut: T = 3mg cos θ for release from the horizontal position.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 N is the tension at the lowest point (θ = 0); 1 N keeps only the component of weight; 2 N is just mg.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wheel starts from rest and, rotating about a fixed axis with uniform angular acceleration, reaches 120 revolutions per minute in 4 s. Its angular acceleration is:

solution.concept: Kinematics of rotation about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: Convert the final rate to rad/s: 120 rev/min = 2 rev/s = 4π rad/s. Then α = (ω − ω₀)/t.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 divides 120 by 4 without converting rev/min; 2π rad/s² doubles the converted angular speed (8π rad/s); π/2 rad/s² halves it (2π rad/s).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', kinematics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: A thin circular ring has mass 0.5 kg and radius 20 cm. Its moment of inertia about an axis that is perpendicular to its plane and passes through a point on the ring is:

solution.concept: Theorem of parallel axes
solution.explanation: About the central axis perpendicular to its plane, I = MR². The required axis is parallel to it at a distance R, so I = MR² + MR² = 2MR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.02 kg m² is the central value; 0.03 kg m² is the value about a tangent lying in the plane of the ring (3MR²/2); 0.01 kg m² is the value about a diameter.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', theorem of parallel axes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Moment of inertia and axis theorems
questions.question_text: The radius of gyration of a thin uniform rod of length L, about an axis perpendicular to the rod through its centre, is:

solution.concept: Radius of gyration
solution.explanation: I = Mk², and for this axis I = ML²/12. Hence k² = L²/12 and k = L/√12 = L/(2√3).
solution.why_others_wrong: L/√3 is the radius of gyration about a perpendicular axis through one end (I = ML²/3); L/2 and L/√2 do not follow from either value of I.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of inertia and radius of gyration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wheel of moment of inertia 2 kg m² about its fixed axle starts from rest. A constant torque of 4 N m acts on it about the axle while it turns through 25 rad. Neglecting friction, its final angular speed is:

solution.concept: Work done by a torque and rotational kinetic energy
solution.explanation: The work done by a constant torque is W = τθ. By the work–energy theorem for rotation it equals the gain in rotational kinetic energy ½Iω².
solution.why_others_wrong: 5√2 rad/s halves the work; 50 rad/s sets ω = τθ/I; 100 rad/s equates ω with the work done.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', work done by a torque

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For every rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the total angular momentum vector points along the axis of rotation.
Statement II: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the component of its angular momentum along that axis is Iω, where I is its moment of inertia about the axis and ω its angular velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Angular momentum of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis
solution.explanation: In general the angular momentum of a body rotating about a fixed axis has a component along the axis and possibly a component perpendicular to it. Only the component along the axis is Iω. For bodies symmetric about the axis the perpendicular part vanishes, but not for every body. So Statement I is false and Statement II is true.
steps: L = L_axis + L_perp; L_perp = 0 only for bodies symmetric about the axis → I false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I overgeneralises the symmetric case, so options calling it true are wrong; Statement II is the standard result, so options calling it false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', angular momentum in case of rotation about a fixed axis
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A force acts on a rigid body that can turn about a fixed axis, in a plane perpendicular to the axis. Match List-I (the force and where it acts) with List-II (magnitude of its torque about the axis).

List-I:
A. 10 N, applied 0.5 m from the axis, perpendicular to the line joining the axis to the point of application
B. 10 N, applied 0.5 m from the axis, at 30° to the line joining the axis to the point of application
C. 20 N, applied 0.4 m from the axis, along the line joining the axis to the point of application
D. 4 N, applied 2 m from the axis, perpendicular to the line joining the axis to the point of application

List-II:
I. 0
II. 2.5 N m
III. 5 N m
IV. 8 N m

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Moment of a force: τ = rF sin θ
solution.explanation: The magnitude of torque is rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between the position vector of the point of application (from the axis) and the force.
solution.why_others_wrong: Matching B to 5 N m or C to 2.5 N m uses cos θ instead of sin θ; a force whose line of action passes through the axis has no torque.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', moment of force (torque)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A wheel of radius 0.5 m starts from rest and rotates about its fixed axle with a uniform angular acceleration of 2 rad/s². At t = 2 s, the magnitude of the total linear acceleration of a point on its rim is:

solution.concept: Tangential and centripetal acceleration of a point of a rotating body
solution.explanation: A rim point has a tangential acceleration αR and a centripetal acceleration ω²R, at right angles to each other. At t = 2 s, ω = αt = 4 rad/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 m/s² is only the centripetal part; 1 m/s² only the tangential part; 9 m/s² adds two perpendicular components as scalars.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A light string is wound round a pulley in the form of a uniform disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.2 m, which rotates without friction about a fixed horizontal axle through its centre. A block of mass 2 kg hangs from the free end of the string and is released from rest. The string does not slip. Taking g = 10 m/s², the angular speed of the pulley when the block has descended 1.2 m is:

solution.concept: Energy conservation for a falling block and a rotating pulley
solution.explanation: The block's loss of potential energy goes into the block's kinetic energy and the pulley's rotational kinetic energy, with I = MR²/2 and v = ωR.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√6 rad/s ignores the pulley's rotational kinetic energy; 10√3 rad/s takes I = MR² (a ring); 4 rad/s is the block's speed in m/s, not the angular speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin uniform square plate has side 2a. One of its four quarters, a square of side a at one corner, is cut away. The centre of mass of the remaining L-shaped plate is shifted from the centre of the original square by a distance:

options.text: a√2/6, away from the removed corner
a√2/3, away from the removed corner

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a body with a part removed
solution.explanation: Treat the remaining plate as three equal squares, each of mass m, with centres at (a/2, a/2), (3a/2, a/2) and (a/2, 3a/2) when the original plate occupies 0 ≤ x, y ≤ 2a and the removed square is the one at the corner (2a, 2a).
steps: Shift = √2 × (a − 5a/6) = a√2/6, along the diagonal away from the removed corner
solution.shortcut: Removing mass m at distance a√2/2 from the centre shifts the CM of the remaining 3m by (m/3m)(a√2/2) = a√2/6 the other way.
solution.why_others_wrong: The centre of mass moves away from the region where mass was removed, not towards it; a√2/3 is twice the correct shift; a/6 gives only one coordinate of the shift.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', centre of mass
solution.final_answer: Option A: a√2/6, away from the removed corner

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A uniform rod standing vertically on a perfectly smooth horizontal floor is slightly disturbed and falls. During the fall its centre of mass moves along a vertical straight line.
Reason (R): The external forces on the rod (its weight and the normal reaction of the smooth floor) are both vertical, so the horizontal component of the acceleration of its centre of mass is zero.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Motion of the centre of mass under external forces
solution.explanation: The centre of mass of a system moves as if all its mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted there. A smooth floor exerts no friction, so there is no horizontal external force. The CM starts with zero horizontal velocity and has zero horizontal acceleration, so it falls straight down (the foot slides sideways instead).
steps: External forces: mg (down), N (up), no friction
a_cm,x = 0 and v_cm,x(0) = 0 → CM moves vertically
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the reason the centre of mass has no horizontal motion, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Blocks of masses 1 kg and 3 kg, connected by a light spring, lie on a smooth horizontal floor. A constant horizontal force of 8 N, along the line of the spring, is applied to the 3 kg block only. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The acceleration of the centre of mass of the system is 2 m/s².
(b) The acceleration of the centre of mass does not depend on how much the spring is stretched or compressed.
(c) The acceleration of the 3 kg block is 8/3 m/s² at every instant.
(d) The total linear momentum of the system increases at the rate of 8 kg m s⁻².
(e) If the force is removed at some instant, the velocity of the centre of mass stays constant after that.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Centre of mass of a system with internal forces
solution.explanation: The spring force is internal: it changes the individual accelerations but not the motion of the centre of mass, which is fixed by the net external force: M a_cm = F_ext = dP/dt.
steps: (b) internal forces do not affect a_cm, true
(c) the 3 kg block also feels the spring force, which varies, so its acceleration is not always 8/3 m/s² → false
(e) no external horizontal force → v_cm constant, true
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) ignore the spring force on the 3 kg block; omitting (b) or (e) misses that internal forces never change the motion of the centre of mass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', motion of centre of mass; linear momentum of a system of particles

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A body weighs 49 N on the Earth's surface, where g = 9.8 m/s². It is taken to a planet where the acceleration due to gravity at the surface is 3.6 m/s². Its mass and its weight on that planet are respectively:

solution.concept: Mass versus weight
solution.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change from place to place; weight is the gravitational force mg and depends on the local g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.8 kg wrongly lets the mass change; '5 kg and 49 N' keeps the weight unchanged; 13.6 kg divides the Earth weight by the planet's g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Taking the zero of potential energy at infinite separation, the gravitational potential energy of a system of two point masses is positive.
Statement II: The gravitational potential energy of a system of two point masses is directly proportional to the distance between them.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Gravitational potential energy of two particles
solution.explanation: U = −Gm₁m₂/r with U = 0 at infinity. It is negative for every finite r (Statement I false) and varies as 1/r, not as r (Statement II false). Its magnitude decreases as r increases, while U itself increases towards zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements contradict U = −Gm₁m₂/r, so every option calling either of them true is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', gravitational potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Because of a small loss of energy, the radius of the circular orbit of a satellite round the Earth decreases by 2%. Its period of revolution:

solution.concept: Kepler's third law for small changes
solution.explanation: For a circular orbit T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2). For a small change, the fractional change in T is 3/2 times the fractional change in r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1% uses T ∝ r^(1/2) (the speed relation); 'increases' gets the sign wrong; 2% assumes T ∝ r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', Kepler's laws; earth satellites

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A satellite orbiting just above the surface of the Earth has period T. A planet has the same mean density as the Earth but twice its radius. Treating both as uniform spheres, the period of a satellite orbiting just above the surface of the planet is:

solution.concept: Period of a close-orbiting satellite in terms of density
solution.explanation: For an orbit of radius R about a uniform sphere, T = 2π√(R³/GM), and M = (4/3)πR³ρ. Substituting, T = √(3π/(Gρ)), which depends only on the density.
steps: = √(3π/(Gρ)) → same ρ gives the same T
solution.why_others_wrong: 2T and √2 T forget that the planet's mass grows as R³; T/2 inverts the dependence.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two satellites of different masses revolve round the Earth in the same circular orbit. Which of the following is different for the two satellites?

solution.concept: Dependence of satellite quantities on the satellite's mass
solution.explanation: From GMm/r² = mv²/r, the orbital speed v = √(GM/r) does not depend on m; so neither does the period 2πr/v nor the acceleration GM/r². The kinetic energy ½mv² = GMm/(2r) is proportional to m.
steps: v, T and a are independent of m
solution.why_others_wrong: Speed, period and centripetal acceleration all cancel the satellite's mass, so they are the same for both satellites.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', earth satellites; energy of an orbiting satellite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Satellite A, of mass 2m, revolves round the Earth in a circular orbit of radius r. Satellite B, of mass m, revolves in a circular orbit of radius 4r. The ratio of the angular momentum of A about the Earth's centre to that of B is:

solution.concept: Angular momentum of a satellite in a circular orbit
solution.explanation: L = m v r with v = √(GM/r), so L = m√(GMr). Compare m√r for the two satellites.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 ignores the masses; 2 : 1 ignores the radii; 1 : 4 uses L ∝ m r instead of m√r.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Imagine a straight narrow tunnel dug along a diameter of the Earth, treated as a uniform sphere of radius 6400 km with g = 10 m/s² at its surface. A small body is released from rest at the mouth of the tunnel. Neglecting air resistance and the Earth's rotation, its speed as it passes the centre of the Earth is:

solution.concept: Gravity inside a uniform Earth: g ∝ distance from the centre
solution.explanation: Inside a uniform Earth, g(r) = g r/R, directed towards the centre, so the body's acceleration is −(g/R)r: simple harmonic motion with ω = √(g/R) and amplitude R. Its maximum speed, at the centre, is ωR = √(gR).
solution.shortcut: Average force method: work done = ∫₀ᴿ m(g r/R) dr = mgR/2 = ½mv² → v = √(gR).
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.2 km/s is the escape speed from the surface; 5.66 km/s is √(gR/2); 4 km/s halves the answer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', acceleration due to gravity below the surface of the earth

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a satellite in a circular orbit round the Earth slowly loses mechanical energy because of a thin atmosphere, it spirals into lower orbits and its orbital speed increases.
Reason (R): The total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r is −GMm/(2r), so a loss of energy means a smaller r, and the orbital speed √(GM/r) is larger for a smaller r.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Energy of an orbiting satellite
solution.explanation: E = −GMm/2r becomes more negative as r decreases; losing energy therefore moves the satellite inward. Its kinetic energy GMm/2r = −E then increases, while its potential energy −GMm/r decreases by twice as much. R states exactly this chain.
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the full reason for the apparently surprising speed-up, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', energy of an orbiting satellite
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A planet moves round the Sun in an elliptical orbit. Its distance from the Sun at aphelion (farthest point) is twice its distance at perihelion (nearest point). Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its angular momentum about the Sun is the same at perihelion and at aphelion.
(b) Its speed at perihelion is twice its speed at aphelion.
(c) Its kinetic energy at perihelion is four times its kinetic energy at aphelion.
(d) The gravitational force on it at perihelion is four times the force at aphelion.
(e) Its total mechanical energy is greater at perihelion than at aphelion.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kepler's second law and conservation laws for an elliptical orbit
solution.explanation: The Sun's force is central, so the planet's angular momentum is conserved (the basis of Kepler's second law). At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so mv_p r_p = mv_a r_a. Gravity is conservative, so total energy is constant.
steps: (e) total energy is the same everywhere on the orbit → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) confuse kinetic energy with total energy; omitting (a) misses the conservation law behind Kepler's second law.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Gravitation', Kepler's laws

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An open vessel contains a 20 cm deep layer of water (density 1000 kg/m³) with a 10 cm deep layer of oil (density 800 kg/m³) floating on it. Taking g = 10 m/s², the gauge pressure at the bottom of the vessel is:

solution.concept: Pressure due to liquid columns
solution.explanation: The gauge pressure at a depth is the weight per unit area of the liquid above. With two layers, add ρgh for each layer.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3000 Pa treats both layers as water; 2400 Pa treats both as oil; 800 Pa counts only the oil layer.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', pressure (variation of pressure with depth)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Wires of equal length and equal cross-section made of the materials below are stretched by equal loads. The extension is least for the wire made of:

solution.concept: Young's modulus and extension
solution.explanation: Extension ΔL = FL/(AY). For equal F, L and A it is least for the largest Young's modulus. Steel (about 2 × 10¹¹ N/m²) has a larger Young's modulus than copper and aluminium, and rubber's is far smaller.
solution.why_others_wrong: Copper and aluminium have smaller Young's moduli than steel, and rubber stretches enormously, so all three extend more.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Young's modulus (table of Young's moduli)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: 200 g of water at 80 °C is mixed with 300 g of water at 30 °C in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. The final temperature of the mixture is:

solution.concept: Principle of calorimetry
solution.explanation: In an insulated system, heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water; the specific heat is the same for both, so it cancels.
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 °C is the plain average of the temperatures; 60 °C swaps the masses; 45 °C is a slip in the weighted average.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', calorimetry

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following has the lowest thermal conductivity?

solution.concept: Thermal conductivity of common materials
solution.explanation: Metals such as copper and steel are good conductors; glass is a poor conductor; still air is a much poorer conductor still (about 0.02 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), which is why trapped air in wool, fibre glass or double windows insulates well.
steps: Copper ≈ 400, steel ≈ 50, glass ≈ 1, still air ≈ 0.02 (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹)
solution.why_others_wrong: Copper and steel conduct heat very well, and glass, though a poor conductor, conducts far better than still air.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', conduction (table of thermal conductivities)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (situation) with List-II (type of stress mainly produced).

List-I:
A. A wire from which a load hangs
B. A solid metal ball resting at the bottom of a deep sea
C. A thick book whose lower face is held fixed while its upper face is pushed sideways
D. A pillar supporting the roof of a building

List-II:
I. Tensile stress
II. Compressive stress
III. Hydraulic stress
IV. Shearing stress

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Kinds of stress
solution.explanation: A pulling force along the length gives tensile stress; a pushing force along the length gives compressive stress; a force tangential to a face gives shearing stress; a uniform pressure from a surrounding fluid on all sides gives hydraulic stress (with a change of volume).
steps: B: fluid pressure all round → hydraulic (III)
D: squeezed along its length → compressive (II)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes confuse the uniform squeeze of a fluid (hydraulic) with the one-directional squeeze of a pillar (compressive), or a sideways push with compression.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', stress and strain
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The breaking stress of a certain steel is 8 × 10⁸ N/m² and its density is 8000 kg/m³. Taking g = 10 m/s², the greatest length of a uniform wire of this steel that can hang vertically from a rigid support without breaking under its own weight is:

solution.concept: Breaking stress of a wire under its own weight
solution.explanation: The stress is greatest at the top of the wire, which supports the weight of the whole wire: stress = (ρALg)/A = ρgL. The wire breaks when this reaches the breaking stress. The cross-section cancels.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 km uses the average stress ρgL/2 instead of the greatest stress at the top; 1 km and 100 km are power-of-ten slips.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', stress–strain curve (fracture point)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two small spheres of the same radius, with densities 9000 kg/m³ and 3000 kg/m³, fall through the same viscous liquid of density 1000 kg/m³. Assuming Stokes' law holds, the ratio of the terminal velocity of the denser sphere to that of the lighter one is:

solution.concept: Terminal velocity: dependence on densities
solution.explanation: At terminal velocity, weight = buoyant force + viscous drag, giving v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η). For equal radii in the same liquid, v_t ∝ (ρ − σ).
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is the ratio of the densities themselves, ignoring buoyancy; 9 squares it; 2 is a slip in subtracting the liquid's density.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', Stokes' law and terminal velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A clean capillary tube of internal radius 0.2 mm stands vertically in a liquid of density 1000 kg/m³ and surface tension 0.04 N/m. The angle of contact between the liquid and the tube is 60°. Taking g = 10 m/s², the height to which the liquid rises in the tube is:

solution.concept: Capillary rise with a non-zero angle of contact
solution.explanation: The upward pull of surface tension around the rim, 2πrS cos θ, supports the weight of the raised column, πr²hρg, so h = 2S cos θ/(rρg).
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 cm ignores cos θ; 1 cm uses the diameter in place of the radius; 2√3 cm uses sin 60° in place of cos 60°.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', capillary rise

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two metal rods P and Q have coefficients of linear expansion 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ and 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ respectively. Their lengths are chosen so that the difference between their lengths is 10 cm at every temperature. The lengths of P and Q are respectively:

solution.concept: Linear expansion: ΔL = Lα ΔT
solution.explanation: The difference stays constant only if both rods expand by the same amount for any temperature change: L_P α_P = L_Q α_Q. The rod with the smaller α must be the longer one.
steps: L_Q − L_P = L_P/3 = 10 cm → L_P = 30 cm, L_Q = 40 cm
solution.why_others_wrong: 40 cm and 30 cm gives the longer length to the rod that expands more, so the difference would grow; the other pairs do not satisfy L_P α_P = L_Q α_Q.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (situation) with List-II (the main mode of heat transfer).

List-I:
A. The handle of a metal spoon left in a cup of hot tea becomes hot
B. A cool breeze blows from the sea towards the land during the day
C. Heat is carried round the human body by the circulating blood
D. Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth

List-II:
I. Conduction
II. Natural convection
III. Forced convection
IV. Radiation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Modes of heat transfer
solution.explanation: In conduction heat passes through the material without bulk motion; in convection the material itself moves. In natural convection the motion is driven by gravity acting on density differences (sea breeze); in forced convection a pump or fan drives it (the heart pumping blood). Radiation needs no medium.
steps: B: warm air over land rises → natural convection
C: heart pumps blood → forced convection
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap natural and forced convection or treat the sea breeze as conduction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Three vessels of very different shapes, with bases of equal area, are filled with water to the same height. The pressure on the base is the same in all three, even though they hold different amounts of water.
Reason (R): The pressure at a depth h below the open surface of a liquid at rest is P = Pₐ + ρgh, which depends only on the depth and not on the shape or cross-section of the vessel.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Hydrostatic paradox
solution.explanation: The pressure at the base depends only on the vertical depth of the liquid above it (and the atmospheric pressure), so equal heights give equal pressures whatever the shape. This is the 'hydrostatic paradox', and R states the law that resolves it.
steps: P = Pₐ + ρgh: same h → same P
solution.why_others_wrong: R is exactly the reason for A, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', variation of pressure with depth (hydrostatic paradox)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The excess pressure inside a soap bubble is twice the excess pressure inside a liquid drop of the same radius, made of a liquid of the same surface tension.
Reason (R): A soap bubble has two liquid–air surfaces (inner and outer), while a liquid drop has only one.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Excess pressure across curved surfaces
solution.explanation: For one curved surface of radius r the excess pressure is 2S/r. A drop has one surface, so ΔP = 2S/r. The thin film of a bubble has two surfaces in series, so ΔP = 2 × 2S/r = 4S/r. R gives the reason for the factor of two.
solution.why_others_wrong: R is precisely why the bubble's excess pressure is doubled, so B is wrong; both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', excess pressure inside a drop and a bubble
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Water flows steadily at 1 m/s through the wide part of a horizontal pipe, which narrows to one-third of that cross-sectional area. Two thin vertical tubes, open at the top, are fitted to the wide and the narrow parts. Treating water as non-viscous and incompressible (density 1000 kg/m³) and taking g = 10 m/s², the difference in the heights of water in the two vertical tubes is:

solution.concept: Equation of continuity with Bernoulli's principle
solution.explanation: Continuity gives the speed in the narrow part; Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe gives the pressure difference; each vertical tube shows its pressure as a water column, so Δh = ΔP/(ρg).
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 cm drops the ½ in ½ρv²; 45 cm forgets v₁ (uses ½ρv₂²); 4 cm is a power-of-ten slip.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Fluids', equation of continuity; Bernoulli's principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: 10 g of steam at 100 °C is passed into an insulated container of negligible heat capacity holding 40 g of ice at 0 °C. All the steam condenses. Take the latent heat of vaporisation of water as 540 cal g⁻¹, the latent heat of fusion of ice as 80 cal g⁻¹ and the specific heat of water as 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The final temperature of the contents is:

solution.concept: Calorimetry with two changes of state
solution.explanation: First check whether all the ice melts: the steam can give 10 × 540 = 5400 cal just by condensing, more than the 40 × 80 = 3200 cal needed to melt the ice. So the final state is 50 g of water at some θ between 0 °C and 100 °C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 °C ignores the cooling of the condensed steam from 100 °C; 80 °C ignores the latent heat of fusion; 100 °C assumes some steam stays uncondensed, contrary to the stem.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', change of state and latent heat; calorimetry

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A solid block of density 4000 kg/m³ hangs from a light steel wire, which is stretched by 1.0 mm. The block is then completely immersed in water (density 1000 kg/m³), still hanging from the wire and not touching the container. Within the elastic limit, the extension of the wire becomes:

solution.concept: Hooke's law combined with buoyancy
solution.explanation: The extension is proportional to the tension. In water the tension is the weight minus the buoyant force: T = Vρg − Vρ_w g = W(1 − ρ_w/ρ).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.25 mm keeps only the buoyant part; 0.80 mm uses a density ratio of 1/5; 1.0 mm ignores the upthrust.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Mechanical Properties of Solids', Hooke's law and Young's modulus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A solid metal sphere, with coefficient of linear expansion 2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, is heated from 20 °C to 120 °C. Which of the following statements are correct (to a good approximation)?

(a) Its radius increases by 0.2%.
(b) Its surface area increases by 0.4%.
(c) Its volume increases by 0.6%.
(d) Its density decreases by about 0.6%.
(e) Its mass increases by 0.6%.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Linear, area and volume expansion
solution.explanation: For small changes, ΔL/L = αΔT, ΔA/A = 2αΔT and ΔV/V = 3αΔT. The mass does not change, so the density falls by the same fraction by which the volume rises.
steps: (e) heating does not change mass → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) confuse volume with mass; leaving out (b), (c) or (d) misses the factors 2 and 3 for area and volume.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', thermal expansion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Two rods of the same cross-section but different thermal conductivities are joined end to end, their sides insulated, and conduct heat in the steady state. The temperature gradient is larger in the rod of smaller thermal conductivity.
Statement II: If the two rods are interchanged, keeping the temperatures of the two free ends unchanged, the rate of heat flow through the combination changes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Steady-state conduction through rods in series
solution.explanation: In the steady state the same heat current H flows through both rods: H = KA (dT/dx). With H and A the same, the gradient dT/dx = H/(KA) is larger where K is smaller (Statement I true). The total thermal resistance L₁/(K₁A) + L₂/(K₂A) does not depend on the order of the rods, so H is unchanged (Statement II false).
steps: Same H in both → dT/dx ∝ 1/K → I true
R_total = R₁ + R₂, order-independent → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Series resistances add in either order, so the options calling II true are wrong; Statement I follows from the equal heat current, so the options calling it false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermal Properties of Matter', conduction (steady state, thermal conductivity)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The temperature of 2 moles of a monatomic ideal gas rises by 50 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, the increase in its internal energy, whatever the process by which the change is made, is:

solution.concept: Internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of temperature only
solution.explanation: For an ideal gas, U depends only on T, so ΔU = nC_vΔT in every process, with C_v = 3R/2 for a monatomic gas.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2075 J uses C_p = 5R/2 (that is the heat at constant pressure); 830 J uses R; 2490 J uses 3R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', internal energy; specific heat capacity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following thermodynamic variables is extensive (depends on the size of the system)?

solution.concept: Extensive and intensive variables
solution.explanation: If a system in equilibrium is divided into two equal parts, an extensive variable (internal energy, mass, volume) is halved in each part, while an intensive variable (pressure, temperature, density) is unchanged.
solution.why_others_wrong: Pressure, temperature and density are the same in each half of a system in equilibrium, so they are intensive.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', thermodynamic state variables

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas undergo, separately, each process in List-I. Take R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Match List-I (process) with List-II (value of the stated quantity).

List-I:
A. Heated at constant volume so that its temperature rises by 10 K: heat absorbed
B. Heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 10 K: work done by the gas
C. Expands isothermally, absorbing 500 J of heat: work done by the gas
D. Expands adiabatically, doing 300 J of work: change in its internal energy

List-II:
I. −300 J
II. 166 J
III. 249 J
IV. 500 J

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: First law of thermodynamics in the four basic processes
solution.explanation: Apply ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW with ΔU = nC_vΔT (C_v = 3R/2 for a monatomic gas). At constant volume no work is done; at constant pressure W = PΔV = nRΔT; isothermally ΔU = 0 so W = Q; adiabatically Q = 0 so ΔU = −W.
steps: C: ΔU = 0 → W = Q = 500 J → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the isochoric heat with the isobaric work, or give the adiabatic ΔU the wrong sign (or treat the isothermal heat as a change in internal energy).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics; thermodynamic processes
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas is taken from state A to state B at constant volume, absorbing 300 J of heat. It is then taken from B to state C at constant pressure, absorbing 500 J of heat and doing 200 J of work. If the gas is instead taken from A to C along a different path in which it does 150 J of work, the heat it absorbs along that path is:

solution.concept: Internal energy as a state function; first law
solution.explanation: Find ΔU from A to C using the first path. ΔU is the same for every path between the same states, so apply the first law on the new path.
steps: New path: Q = ΔU + W = 600 + 150 = 750 J
solution.why_others_wrong: 800 J adds the heats of the first path, as if heat were a state function; 600 J forgets the work on the new path; 450 J subtracts the work instead of adding it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: 1 g of water at 100 °C, occupying 1 cm³, is converted into 1701 cm³ of steam at 100 °C at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2260 J g⁻¹. The work done by the system and the increase in its internal energy are respectively:

solution.concept: First law applied to a change of state
solution.explanation: The heat supplied is the latent heat, 2260 J. Part of it is used as work against the constant external pressure while the volume grows by 1700 cm³; the rest increases the internal energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2430 J adds the work instead of subtracting it; '0 and 2260 J' ignores the expansion; '2260 J and 170 J' swaps the two quantities.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.subtopic: Second law, reversible and irreversible processes
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Heat can flow by itself, with no other effect, from a colder body to a hotter body.
Statement II: After a system has undergone an irreversible process, it can never be brought back to its initial state by any means.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Second law of thermodynamics and irreversible processes
solution.explanation: Statement I contradicts the Clausius statement of the second law: heat cannot pass from a colder to a hotter body as the sole result of a process. Statement II misreads 'irreversible': the system itself can be returned to its initial state (for example, a freely expanded gas can be compressed back), but not without leaving some change in the surroundings, such as work done on the system or heat given to a reservoir.
steps: I violates the Clausius statement → false
II: the system can be restored, only the surroundings cannot also be restored with no other change → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Irreversibility means the system and the surroundings cannot both be restored with no other change anywhere; it does not mean the system alone can never return. Statement I is false because heat does not flow by itself from a colder to a hotter body.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', second law of thermodynamics; reversible and irreversible processes
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When an ideal gas expands at constant pressure, its internal energy decreases.
Reason (R): The internal energy of a given amount of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Internal energy in an isobaric process
solution.explanation: At constant pressure, V/T is constant for an ideal gas, so an expansion (V increasing) means a rise in temperature. Since U depends only on T (R is true), U increases: A is false.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C (which all call A true) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', internal energy; thermodynamic processes
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A monatomic ideal gas is heated in a process during which the work done by the gas is always half the heat supplied to it. The molar heat capacity of the gas in this process is (R is the gas constant):

solution.concept: Molar heat capacity for a general process from the first law
